results.question: Compare what the book says about making your own chroma keyer with what it says about nons
results.answer:
The books discuss these as two unrelated problems — one about color, one about geometry — and the only connection is that both demand care when you composite, though only one of them is something the authors think you should build yourself.

**Chroma keying: understand it, but buy it**

A chroma keyer converts RGB to an HSV-style representation internally because saturation isn't an RGB attribute; it then sets a center color and carves out hue, saturation, and value ranges around it, with tolerances for a soft-edged matte [S3]. The simpler version just picks a color range and treats every pixel inside it as background, with extra controls for saturation and luminance [S4].

On building your own, the book is blunt: unlike a homemade luma keyer, where cleverness can bring real improvements, "making your own chroma keyer will probably be more hassle than it's worth" — an off-the-shelf unit is hard to improve upon [S1]. If you insist, the recipe is to convert RGB to HSV and pipe it through a color curve, where the red curve now carries hue, green carries saturation, and blue carries value; adjusting the three curves includes or excludes the target's ranges [S2]. A more interesting homemade variant is a 3D color keyer that plots pixels in the RGB cube on simplified Primatte principles, keying on any arbitrary color rather than a single hue [S8]. The commercial tools the sources praise — Primatte and Keylight — are exactly the off-the-shelf kind [S14].

**Nonsquare pixels: respect them, don't reinvent them**

A nonsquare pixel is simply one whose width doesn't equal its height, quantified by pixel aspect ratio [S9][S6]. These formats exist because the aspect ratio of the image as displayed differs from the original digital image [S6]; SD video uses rectangular pixels (720×480 NTSC, 720×576 PAL) while HD, graphics software, and monitors use square ones [S10]. Display systems can temporarily "unsqueeze" an image so it looks correct on screen without touching the underlying data [S5].

The practical warning, using Cinemascope's dramatic 2:1 squeeze as the example: operations like rotation must happen in unsqueezed space, or geometry distorts — even a 5° rotation on a squeezed image produces subtle errors that show up on a round subject [S13][S7].

**Where they meet**

**What the sources do not say:** none of the evidence connects nonsquare pixels to chroma keying specifically. The closest bridge is the general compositing advice — if you key an element from a squeezed format, any rotation or geometric operation on it has to account for the pixel shape, or the matted subject will look wrong [S13]. Nothing in the corpus claims that pixel shape affects how a keyer reads hue or saturation. One adjacent warning worth flagging: the "full-resolution luminance, half-size chroma" encoding the sources describe is chroma *subsampling* for compression, not chroma keying, and not a pixel-shape issue [S11].

So the contrast in the books: chroma keying is a tool you could theoretically assemble from curves but shouldn't bother to, while nonsquare pixels are a format constraint you can't avoid and must actively manage. One rewards buying the commercial solution; the other rewards understanding the geometry underneath.

results.question: Compare what the book says about miscellaneous drawing tips with what it says about transc
results.answer:
The two discussions answer the same underlying question — when do you fix colors in place, and when do you start over — but from opposite ends of the workflow. The drawing tips treat color as a matter of artistic taste; the transcoding-versus-rerendering material treats it as a matter of technical fidelity. In this corpus they come from different books: the manga how-to guides cover the drawing tips [S4][S5], while the VES Handbook and compositing texts cover color conversion [S1][S2][S6].

| Dimension | Drawing tips | Transcoding vs. color rerendering |
|---|---|---|
| **Goal** | Find a stronger, more pleasing color combination, or add effects like luminous circles [S4] | Reproduce the same perceived colors on a different display, matching the original as closely as possible [S3] |
| **Trigger** | Subjective: the color "isn't quite to your liking" near completion [S4] | Objective: the degree of difference between displays — gamma, primary chromaticities, luminance, viewing conditions [S2] |
| **Cheap fix** | Swap colors freely; digital tools let you test a color, reject it, and immediately try another [S5] | Transcode when displays are nearly identical: linearize the encoded RGB, convert to CIE XYZ, convert to the second display's RGB, re-apply the encoding curve [S2] |
| **Thorough fix** | Redraw the entire picture from scratch, since hand-drawn revision is impractical [S5] | Color rerender when conditions are grossly dissimilar: undo the first display's color rendering, then re-render the CIE XYZ values for the new display [S1] |

The parallel is the decision rule: when the two situations are close, an in-place correction works; when they diverge fundamentally, the only correct fix is to return to a neutral, pre-rendered foundation — CIE XYZ values in the color pipeline, a blank page in drawing — and redo the rendering [S1][S5]. The tone differs sharply, though: for color science the choice is a computed, cost-based decision, whereas for the hand artist the threat of redoing is so real that it shapes the creative mindset itself, turning "no takebacks" into a live-performance tension [S5].

The two bodies of text never overlap — the drawing books say nothing about color spaces or gamma, and the color-science sources say nothing about artistic intent — so the cost-and-fidelity parallel above is the synthesis, not something either source states.

results.question: Compare what the book says about transcoding versus color rerendering with what it says ab
results.answer:
The Handbook draws a clean, practical line between the two: **transcoding** re-encodes an image for a new display while assuming the two displays are essentially equivalent, whereas **color rerendering** abandons that assumption and rebuilds the image's color for the new viewing environment. The corpus, however, contains nothing about FACE OFF — the phrase, the film, or the concept — so that side of the comparison must be flagged as missing rather than invented, and only its nearest neighbor, digital face *morphing*, can be grounded.

## The two color processes

Transcoding is the cheaper operation. When black levels, white luminance, viewing conditions, and gamma are identical between displays and only the primary chromaticities differ, you linearize the first display's encoded RGB, convert to CIE XYZ, convert to the second display's RGB, and re-impose the encoding nonlinearity [S2]. It is a mechanical re-encoding of the same image data. Color rerendering is the heavier operation: when contrast, white levels, or viewing conditions are grossly dissimilar, any color rendering done for the first display is undone, and the non-color-rendered CIE XYZ values are then re-rendered for the second display [S1]. Underneath both sits the general definition of *color rendering* — the transformation that accounts for differences in viewing environment, such as a JPEG camera compressing desert-sunlight intensity down to an office monitor's far dimmer peak white [S3], while raw formats defer that step downstream so an effects team can perform it before theatrical release [S5].

## FACE OFF: absent from the corpus

No retrieved material discusses FACE OFF, so I cannot say what the book says about it. The closest item is a compositing passage on face *morphing*: morphing a face onto a car works by creatively matching features (eyes to headlights, mouth to a grill), but morphing onto a featureless target like a baseball fails — the pupil simply dissolves into white leather, producing what the text calls a "mangled dissolve" [S9]. The only other face-related hits are bare bibliographic references to face reenactment and expression-editing papers (ICface, MagicFace) with no content retrieved, and the corpus offers no general discussion of how different methods transform or reinterpret visual media. A comparison restricted to what the evidence actually supports:

| Process | Core operation | When to use | Grounding |
|---|---|---|---|
| Transcoding | Linearize → XYZ → target RGB → re-encode | Displays nearly identical; only primaries differ | [S2] |
| Color rerendering | Undo first display's rendering, re-render XYZ for second | Grossly dissimilar displays or viewing conditions | [S1] |
| Face-off (morphing) | Feature-matched interpolation between two images | Compositing a face transformation; fails without matching features | [S9] |

The practical rule that follows: transcode when the displays are close in black level, white luminance, gamma, and viewing environment, because it preserves the intended look cheaply [S2]; go to full rerendering when the target genuinely differs, because transcoding cannot bridge the gap [S1]. Production pipelines already implement this split — ACES separates the artistic look (RRT) from per-display adaptation (ODT) [S12], and scene-referred OpenEXR playback applies the display transform at load time or as a GPU shader when streaming from disk [S6]. The Handbook also warns that color rendering baked in by a camera in a non-raw format is harder to undo than to perform downstream [S5] — a caution that applies whichever of the two pathways you choose.

results.question: Compare what the book says about affect, fatigue, and injury are control states with what
results.answer:
Strictly, the two halves of this comparison come from different texts in the corpus: the affect/fatigue/injury-as-control-states model lives in the handbook, while object-with-background movement lives in the cinema sources (Block's *Visual Story*, the VES handbook, Mascelli). Read together they are two halves of one pipeline rather than competing accounts — internal state drives movement, and the object–background relationship shapes how that movement is perceived.

```
internal state (affect / fatigue / injury)   →   body as medium   →   execution   →   frame (object vs background)   →   viewer
        [S8, S11, S1]                            [S7]                          [S1, S11]        [S5, S10, S14]                 [S2]
```

**The control-state model.** The handbook defines affect, fatigue, and injury as states that must change later action selection and execution — "not adjectives appended after choreography is chosen" [S8]. Affect is updated by appraisal: an event is scored for goal congruence, controllability, and certainty, and the resulting shift in valence/arousal/dominance produces behavioral effects like narrowed attention, urgent recovery, and a one-attempt rise in risk tolerance [S8]. Its movement-facing fields are concrete kinematics: initiation latency, acceleration profile, posture amplitude, gaze allocation, willingness to accept unstable support, and recovery patience versus urgency [S3].

Fatigue splits into global exertion (RPE, breath cycle, recovery rate) and per-limb local capacity, with coordination effects stated as measurable execution changes — step-width variability, longer stabilization after hard redirection, trunk compensation when the right shoulder is taxed [S11]. Injury specifies mechanical consequences per capacity (load acceptance, flexion tolerance, push-off) plus compensations (favoring the right leg, shortening left stance, increasing trunk lean), and honestly declares its own epistemic status: "dramatic annotation, not clinical measurement," at 0.70 confidence [S1]. The combat-state table generalizes the pattern by giving every object update triggers — effort, impact, rest for fatigue; impact, aggravation, recovery for injury; event appraisal for emotion [S6].

**Object movement against a background.** The cinema sources treat this as a perceptual and optical relationship rather than a physiological one. Induced movement is the key mechanism: a moving object can transfer its movement to a nearby stationary object, and the viewer then attributes the motion to the background while the moving object appears stationary [S5]. The same relativity appears in compositing, where match moving requires the background to be moved to match tracking data extracted from the foreground [S10], and in staging, where moving players between or past foreground objects deliberately generates motion parallax — differential image travel at different distances — to convey position and distance [S14]. The cinema passage closest to the handbook's logic is Block on quality: shots are judged by affinity of movement direction and curve, and sameness of both lowers visual intensity [S2] — a measurable, feature-based judgment, but one whose criterion is the visual relationship among shots, not the mover's internal state.

**Where they meet and where they part.**

| Aspect | Control states (handbook) | Object vs background (cinema) |
|---|---|---|
| Locus | inside the mover | in the frame |
| Causal direction | state → execution | motion → attribution |
| What movement is for | expressing and honoring internal condition | communicating position, distance, spatial story |
| Time scale | appraisal events, effort accumulation, recovery | per shot, per frame |
| Epistemic framing | uncertainty declared (0.70) [S1] | optical fact (tracked, projected) [S10] |

They agree on the essential claim: movement is structure, not decoration — the handbook's states are not appended adjectives [S8], and cinema's quality is a function of measurable direction and curve [S2]. Both also embed movement in a relationship: the body to its support (willingness to accept unstable support [S3]; compensations reweighted across legs and trunk [S1]) versus the object to its background. The Timing for Animation observation that a "train of cause and effect" runs through a body under force [S7] reads like the connective tissue between the two: the state is the force, the body the flexible medium, and the object–background frame the place where the result becomes visible.

They diverge on what movement is for. The handbook's movement must be honest — execution has to change so the body does not contradict its state; cinema's movement must be legible — the frame has to change so the audience reads space clearly, even if that means reassigning the source of motion entirely, as induced movement does [S5]. Practical implication: an animator would generate the shortened left stance and lengthened stabilization from the control state, then compose parallax, tracking, and shot affinity so an audience reads that movement against the background. Laban Effort-and-Shape notation is the shared vocabulary that lets the two layers talk — it is used for affective movement generation [S4] and appears in the handbook's own BESS state framework (awake, dreamlike, distant, near, stable, mobile) [S13].

**Missing link:** the corpus does not address how a system's internal state influences its perception of external objects — for instance, how narrowed attention [S8] would change what a character notices in the background. The connection runs one way in the sources, internal state → movement → viewer perception; the reverse direction, state changing perception of the scene, is unstated.

results.question: Compare what the book says about movement of an object with a background with what it says
results.answer:
Both threads in these texts rest on the same underlying idea — **figure against ground** — but they apply it differently: object motion against a background is treated as a *visual rhythm* problem, while sound editing is treated as a *continuity and perspective* problem. The visual thread asks "how does the moving subject articulate the space," and the sound thread asks "how does the mix keep the scene coherent and weighted."

**What the sources say about object motion against a background.** Bruce Block's *The Visual Story* is the clearest statement: as a moving object passes stationary foreground or background objects, it strengthens the existing visual beat created by those objects, and adding more FG/BG objects increases alternation, repetition, and tempo [S3]. The VES Handbook gives the technical counterpart — when the foreground (camera or subject) moves, the background must move appropriately, a process called match moving, in which tracking data from the foreground image is applied to the background during compositing [S9]; in virtual-studio setups, a keyed foreground is mixed in real time with a photographic or 3D background, with the matched movement automated once the system is calibrated [S11]. So the visual principle is: the background is the stable grid, and the moving object's passage across it creates and punctuates rhythm.

**What the sources say about sound editing.** The sound thread is richer and spans several books, but it clusters around four principles:

- **Perspective and proximity** — levels are mixed to match objects' distance from the action and their narrative importance; as a subject moves closer or farther, volume and panning shift accordingly, and a close-up can justify a louder sound because the shot magnifies the object's size [S1][S10].
- **Continuity across cuts** — if a scene is one place and time, sound should carry consistently from shot to shot: an airplane heard in one shot remains audible (at slightly lowered volume) in the next even if unseen [S4]; walla tracks provide continuous background that blends cuts [S6]; because the ear registers a sound cut more readily than a gradual change, ambience shifts are done as dissolves rather than hard cuts [S8].
- **Layering** — Murch's vertical dimension: the editor thinks simultaneously about what sounds occur at the same time (freeway, birds, plane, footsteps), weaving a multidimensional tapestry rather than a single line [S2]; this is the auditory equivalent of stacking objects in frame.
- **Constructed and motivated sound** — realistic sound alone is often insufficient, so a sound object is built from several unrelated elements (Raging Bull's fights layer beef hits, ripping, water, and airplane roars) [S7]; sound can also motivate a cut, as the teakettle whistle drives the cut to a close-up [S10], or bridge it, as the train whistle starts under the farmer shot and is only revealed as a train after the cut [S14].

**The comparison.**

| Dimension | Object motion vs. background | Sound editing |
|---|---|---|
| Core principle | Moving subject against stationary FG/BG objects creates and strengthens visual beats [S3] | Figure/background layering of simultaneous sounds, with perspective matched to proximity and narrative weight [S1][S13] |
| Continuity | Background must track the foreground's movement exactly (match moving) [S9][S11] | Ambience must survive cuts (airplane, walla); ambience changes are dissolved, not cut [S4][S6][S8] |
| Emphasis and transition | Passing a stationary object makes an existing visual beat stronger [S3] | Sound motivates cuts (kettle) and leads them (train whistles as a sound bridge) [S10][S14] |
| Density and layering | More FG/BG objects = more alternation, repetition, tempo [S3] | Vertical stacks of simultaneous layers — freeway, birds, plane, footsteps — and multi-element constructed sound objects [S2][S7] |

**How each contributes to scene meaning.** Visually, the moving object against the background controls energy and tempo — the scene's rhythm is defined by where and how often the subject crosses the fixed elements of frame [S3]. Sonically, the equivalent work is spatial and attentional: matching sound to proximity tells the viewer where they stand relative to the action [S1][S10], continuous ambience keeps the scene spatially believable from shot to shot [S4][S8], and motivated or bridged sound directs the viewer's attention to what matters next [S10][S14]. In both cases, the goal is the same — making cuts invisible to perception by keeping a stable ground (visual or auditory) that the moving element articulates against.

One gap in the evidence: none of the sources explicitly theorizes how the visual and auditory systems *coordinate with each other* to jointly convey meaning — each discipline is described in its own terms, and the parallel between a moving object's visual beat and a sound's figure/background role has to be inferred rather than cited directly.

results.question: Compare what the book says about sound editing with what it says about write radio sparely
results.answer:
Both bodies of advice land on the same principle — say only what's needed, and say it clearly — but they apply it at opposite ends of production: the radio writer economizes **before** anything is recorded, while the sound editor cleans and refines **after** the material exists.

| | Write radio sparely (Hey Whipple) | Sound editing (Grammar of the Edit, Dancyger, DaVinci Resolve) |
|---|---|---|
| Core rule | Fewer words; spare copy lets talent read slowly, quietly, one word at a time [S1] | Start from the cleanest, clearest, strongest audio signal; degrade it deliberately only if the story demands it [S8] |
| What gets removed | Excess words, before anyone records them — a fat script means editing under studio pressure and without client approval [S2] | "Ums," "ahs," and unwanted sounds, with room tone or B-roll masking the holes; words replaced and levels balanced for clarity [S15][S7] |
| Minimum bar | Spare writing is the norm even for non-bare-bones ideas [S2] | No more dialogue than absolutely necessary; atmosphere, sound effects, and music carry the rest [S12] |
| Warning | Don't over-write [S2] | Don't overdo sound effects, or expect them to do what they can't [S9] |
| Final check | Read the copy aloud to expose awkward constructions and wire-thin segues [S6] | Final phase punctuates meaning — either establishing a point without question or emphasizing a scene's ambiguity [S5] |

The shared spine is subtraction in service of the listener's ear. Hey Whipple calls a fat script the worst studio scenario because you'd be forced to edit under pressure without client approval [S2], and Dancyger applies the same logic to the sound edit — trim dialogue to the necessary minimum, with believability established in the rough cut and dramatic emphasis saved for the fine cut [S12][S14].

The key difference is **where** the economy happens. Radio writing is pre-emptive: the spare script is the raw material handed to the voice talent [S1]. Sound editing is remedial and additive — it cleans what was already recorded, but it also builds: asynchronous sound adds depth through counterpoint with the image, and the final phase adds a music track that translates the film's underlying emotions [S5][S12]. One discipline trims to shape the performance; the other trims, then layers.

results.question: Compare what the book says about write radio sparely with what it says about rewards of go
results.answer:
Two different books on two different subjects — yet the "write radio sparely" advice in *Hey Whipple Squeeze This* and the "rewards of good type development" argument in *Gifts Differing* are both claims that mastery is earned through disciplined effort. The radio rule says the power of an ad comes from what you leave out; the type rule says the power of a person comes from strengths you deliberately build in.

| | Write radio sparely | Rewards of good type development |
|---|---|---|
| **Core rule** | Underwrite — overwriting is "the most common mistake" in radio [S6] | Develop type strengths through effortful excellence, or you keep only your type's weaknesses [S8] |
| **Mechanism** | Fewer words let voice talent read slowly, quietly, one word at a time; silence acts as white space [S1][S11] | Striving that earns real satisfaction, with incentives matched to type — praise for feeling types, freedom for intuitives, dignity for thinkers, possessions for sensing types [S7] |
| **Reward** | A bare-bones spot that "leaps out of the radio"; a skill so rare a radio writer is called "like gold" [S11][S5] | "Profound influence on effectiveness, success, happiness, and mental health" [S4] |
| **Failure mode** | Overwriting — too many words, and promo tags eat whatever time remains [S6][S3] | Inadequate development — "characteristic weaknesses of their type, but not much else" [S8] |

**Where the two ideas meet**

Both treat the payoff as something **earned, not asserted**. Silence "enlarges the idea it surrounds" [S11], just as developed strengths enlarge the person who has them [S4]. Both also frame the discipline as rare: good radio writing is "writing in its most pure form," and a copywriter who can do radio is "like gold" [S5], while good type development is a variable with "great advantage" and wide-ranging influence on effectiveness, success, happiness, and mental health [S4].

They even share a workmanlike streak. The radio advice is bluntly practical — write the mandatories (legal copy, promotional tags) as sparely as possible and time them first, then fit the creative into what's left [S6][S3] — and *Gifts Differing* grounds type development in "excellence in almost anything that children can, with effort, do well," citing Jung's line that a child who has "planted a cabbage right" has "saved the world in that spot" [S7]. Both books are saying: do the unglamorous fundamentals excellently, and the reward follows.

**Where they diverge**

The direction of the work is opposite. Spare writing **subtracts** — cut words, leave silence [S1][S11] — whereas type development **adds** — build strengths, earn rewards [S7][S4]. One is an external craft rule with an immediate, measurable constraint (the :30 clock, the client's tag [S3][S6]); the other is an internal, lifelong process measured in outcomes like success and mental health [S4]. And the beneficiary differs: spareness serves the listener, whose imagination completes the spot — radio "draws on the imaginations of your listeners to get a strong, personal message across" [S10] — while type development serves the person themselves.

**Practical implications for storytelling**

Combined, the two give a storyteller a working philosophy. Sparely: shape the message by what you withhold, trusting silence and the listener's imagination to do the work [S11][S10], and remember that a great spot only pays off with repetition — radio needs frequency to be effective [S14]. Develop: become the writer whose own strengths are mature enough that restraint reads as confidence rather than poverty. That is the synthesis — the craft book tells you how to shape the moment; the development book tells you what the disciplined writer is supposed to be earning, the author's gratification of making "happen what didn't happen but should have" [S12].

One gap in the corpus: nothing directly addresses how deliberate restraint in expression affects audience perception — the silence-as-white-space claim is a practitioner's assertion, not a tested finding [S11].
